title: Culturally adapted psychoeducation (CaPE) for African and Caribbean persons with bipolar disorder in the UK
official: Culturally adapted psychoeducation for African and Caribbean persons with bipolar disorder in the UK: A feasibility study
summary:
Background and study aims
Mental health support in the UK is not always culturally adapted for people from ethnic minority backgrounds who experience mental health challenges, such as bipolar. This study will explore whether offering a Culturally adapted PsychoEducation programme (CaPE) is helpful and appropriate for adults of African and Caribbean heritage living with bipolar in the UK. Participants will either receive the programme alongside their usual routine care, or they will receive their usual care on its own.
This is a feasibility study, which means we are testing out whether the CaPE programme can be delivered successfully and whether people are willing to join and remain in the study. This means that the study may be paused, modified, or stopped earlier than planned. If this happens, participants will be informed about how this impacts them during their participation in the study.
The CaPE programme manual will be developed and improved throughout the study. We will ask participants, therapists, and members of our Research Advisory Group to share their experiences of taking part. Their feedback will help us understand what works well and what could be improved.
Because of this, the manual may change in line with feedback received as the study progresses. This approach helps us make sure the programme reflects what African and Caribbean people living with bipolar disorder say is most helpful and important to them. What we learn will also help us design future support that better meets the needs and preferences of the communities involved.

Who can participate?
We are inviting any person with an African and/or Caribbean ethnic background with a pre-existing diagnosis of any type of bipolar, between the ages of 18 and 60 years, and currently living in the North-West or London. 
You will not be able to take part if you:
•	Are currently experiencing a severe episode of bipolar
•	Have other co-occurring mental health conditions or a severe cognitive impairment that may make it hard to take part in the study
•	Are currently experiencing thoughts of harming yourself or others

What does the study involve?
A Research Support Assistant will meet with you to provide our information sheet and answer any questions that you might have about the study. If you agree to take part, you will be invited to an appointment to sign our study consent form.

You will then be asked to complete some questionnaires to check whether your current mood and mental health meet the study criteria for inclusion. The appointment may last around 30-45 minutes. During the appointment, you will be informed of whether you meet the criteria.
If you meet the study criteria, you will be randomly allocated to one of two possible groups: treatment as usual group (which means to continue with the usual care provided at your General Practice) or the CaPE programme plus treatment as usual group. The CaPE intervention group will be offered 12 weekly online group sessions, each lasting 60 minutes, delivered by trained therapists.
All participants will be asked to complete questionnaires across three time points: at the start of the study, at the end of the intervention (12 weeks) and 3 months after the end of the intervention. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? - We do not expect any significant risks from taking part. While you may not benefit directly, we hope that your participation might help to develop future culturally adapted interventions for bipolar in African and Caribbean communities. All participants from both the CaPE programme group and treatment as usual group will receive vouchers as compensation for their time commitment to the research activities.
Where is the study run from? - Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
August 2026 to July 2027.

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) (UK). 

Who is the main contact?
Ellie Taylor, Research Support Assistant, Ellie.Taylor@lscft.nhs.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Adults aged 18–60 years
2.	Self-identified Black British, Black African, Caribbean, or mixed African/Caribbean heritage
3.	A confirmed diagnosis of bipolar I or II, established through existing clinical records and GP or community mental health teams 
4.	Clinically stable enough to participate, as determined through screening measures
5.	Willing and able to engage with mental health services
6.	Resident within the study catchment area (North West England or London)
7.	Able to provide written informed consent and speak English sufficiently to participate in remote group sessions and complete study assessments
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Current severe mood episode, indicated by screening scores above the study thresholds (e.g., YMRS >38 or PHQ-9 >25)
2.	Active suicidality or immediate risk of harm to self or others
3.	Severe cognitive impairment that would prevent meaningful participation in group sessions or completion of study assessments
4.	Comorbid psychiatric conditions that would interfere with participation in a structured psychoeducation programme (e.g., active psychosis, severe personality disorder, or substance dependence requiring urgent treatment)
5.	Any clinical or safeguarding concern identified during screening that, in the judgement of the research team or clinical referrer, would make participation unsafe or inappropriate at that time
